chief_complaint: throat pain, high fever, fatigue, tonsil exudates
hpi_details: A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with throat pain, high fever, fatigue, tonsil exudates. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he contracted a severe case of strep throat from sharing drinks with an unwell coworker.
concerns: He is worried that his throat will swell shut to the point where he cannot swallow liquids or breathe comfortably.
expectations: He hopes the doctor will perform a throat swab and prescribe strong antibiotics or a steroid shot to knock out the infection fast.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Infectious Mononucleosis (pharyngitis) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management follows a stepwise approach for infectious mononucleosis (pharyngitis): symptomatic care, rest, and avoiding contact sports due to splenic-rupture risk, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: throat pain, high fever, fatigue, tonsil exudates

Key HPI features: A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with throat pain, high fever, fatigue, tonsil exudates. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Fever, exudative tonsillar pharyngitis, tender bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy; abdomen assessed for hepatosplenomegaly.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Infectious Mononucleosis (pharyngitis).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Streptococcal pharyngitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Splenic symptoms.
management_principles: Evaluate for streptococcal pharyngitis and infectious mononucleosis with appropriate testing, provide supportive care, and restrict contact/collision sports while splenic enlargement or acute illness is a concern
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with throat pain, high fever, fatigue, and tonsil exudates. 29M reports symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening.
reference_soap.objective: Fever, exudative tonsillar pharyngitis, tender bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy; abdomen assessed for hepatosplenomegaly.
reference_soap.assessment: Infectious mononucleosis (pharyngitis), with streptococcal pharyngitis as the key differential to exclude.
reference_soap.plan: Evaluate for streptococcal pharyngitis and infectious mononucleosis with appropriate testing, and assess for hepatosplenomegaly. Provide hydration, analgesia/antipyretics, and rest. Restrict contact/collision sports during acute illness and until clinically cleared because of splenic-rupture risk. Seek urgent evaluation for airway compromise, severe abdominal pain, or marked dehydration.

It started about four days ago with a mild scratchy throat and low energy, and it has become much worse since then.
The pain is severe, around an 8 out of 10, and it feels equally intense on both sides of my throat.
Swallowing anything solid hurts badly, but I can still swallow water and I am not drooling.
My breathing is completely normal, with no noisy sounds, and my voice sounds the same as usual.
No, I can open my mouth all the way without any stiffness or spasm in my jaw.
I have had a high fever reaching around 39 degrees Celsius and frequent chills since this began.
No, I haven't had any cough, runny nose, stuffy nose, or red eyes.
Yes, I noticed tender, swollen lumps on both sides of my neck, particularly toward the back of my neck.
No, I haven't seen any rash or rough skin anywhere on my body.
I feel totally drained and have barely been able to get out of bed, but I don't have any pain in my upper left belly.
No, the pain stays right in my throat and does not radiate up into my ears.
A coworker had a bad sore throat a couple of weeks ago, but no one at home is sick.
I rarely ever get sick and have not had a sore throat or tonsil infection like this since high school.
No, I don't suffer from heartburn, acid reflux, or a constant urge to clear my throat.
I checked in the mirror with my phone flashlight and saw my tonsils look swollen, bright red, and covered in white patches.
I thought I must have caught a severe case of strep throat after sharing a drink with a sick friend over the weekend.
The pain is so unbearable that I'm terrified my throat will swell shut and I won't even be able to breathe or drink water.
No, I don't have any immune deficiency, HIV, or chronic medical conditions that weaken my immune system.
My past medical history is completely unremarkable.
I have never had any surgeries and I have never been admitted to a hospital.
I only took some over-the-counter acetaminophen for the fever, which brought it down just a little.
I don't have any drug allergies, and I've taken penicillin antibiotics in the past without problems.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.

There is no significant family history of chronic illness or recurrent infections; my parents are both healthy.

exam.finding: Temperature 38.8°C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, oxygen saturation 98% on ambient air.
The patient appears fatigued and acutely ill with flushed cheeks, but is alert, sitting upright, and in no respiratory distress.
Bilateral tonsils are markedly enlarged and erythematous with thick white exudates; uvula is midline without soft palate asymmetry.
Tender, enlarged bilateral posterior and anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, mobile and without overlying erythema.
Abdomen is soft and non-tender throughout, with no involuntary guarding or rebound tenderness.
Mild splenomegaly with a palpable splenic edge 1 cm below the left costal margin on deep inspiration; liver edge is not palpable.
No maculopapular rash, petechiae, or sandpapery skin lesions are observed on the trunk or extremities.
